title: At-Takathur: more
hookLine: the race for more distracts you until the grave (Surah 102)
last: THE FOUR — FAITH, GOOD, TRUTH, PATIENCE.

lines: FIFTEEN DOLLARS MORE FOR FREE SHIPPING.
cards: The cart has three things in it. Then a banner: free shipping if you spend fifteen dollars more. So you add a fourth thing you didn't want five seconds ago.
More followers, a bigger house, a better phone, one more episode. Not because any of it is bad, but because more has its own pull, and it never says enough.
Today's surah is eight lines about that pull, and its opening runs straight to the graveyard.

teach.b: Surah one hundred two, in Pickthall's translation, begins: Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you Until ye come to the graves. Takathur comes from the root k-th-r, the same root as al-Kawthar a few days ago.
Abundance was a gift. Takathur is a race: competing to have more, piling up to outdo each other. The difference is direction.
One looks at what you were given; the other looks sideways, at what the neighbor has. Commentators tell of two clans in Mecca who boasted about which had more men.
When they ran out of the living, they went to the graveyard and counted the dead.

teach.h: COUNTING, ALL THE WAY TO THE GRAVES.
teach.b: Whether or not that story fits exactly, the surah's picture is sharp: the race for more keeps you busy right up until you visit the graves, and then you're in one.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited this surah and said, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: the son of Adam says, my wealth, my wealth.

teach.h: WHAT YOU ATE, WORE, AND GAVE.
teach.b: But what do you really have of your wealth, except what you ate and used up, what you wore and wore out, or what you gave in charity and sent ahead?
In another hadith, in Bukhari, he said that a person with a valley full of gold would want a second.
The surah ends with being asked, on that Day, about the pleasures you were given.
Some commentators read it as a question of gratitude, not a ban on enjoying them: did you notice them, or were you too busy chasing the next one?

how: Muslims recite at-Takathur in the prayers and often quote it, with the hadith of 'my wealth, my wealth,' as a reminder against competing in possessions.

o: the race to pile up more than others
a quiet night spent in prayer
saving carefully for the hard times ahead

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: what you ate, wore and gave

s: takathur and kawthar share a root
k-th-r, much. one is a gift; the other is a race.
the surah says enjoying pleasures is a sin
it says you'll be asked about them: did you notice them?
the hadith says your wealth is what you saved
it's what you ate, wore, and gave in charity.

games.q: the son of Adam says: my wealth, my wealth. what does the Prophet say he actually has of it?
o: what he ate, what he wore out, and what he gave in charity
games.why: only what he used and what he gave away and 'sent ahead' (Sahih Muslim). the rest was never really his.

practice: Think of one thing you've been meaning to buy, and ask honestly: do I need this, or do I want more? Either answer is fine.
Then find one thing you already have and have stopped noticing, a mug you love, a warm coat, a window, and look at it the way you looked at the thing you wanted.

wordCard.voice: At-Takathur. The race for more, piling up to outdo each other; the name of Surah one hundred two. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: competing in increase, the race for more, from k-th-r.

carryVoice: Your line: more is a distraction. What you keep is what you used and what you gave. That's day one hundred seventy-three.

sources.q: Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you Until ye come to the graves.
